subject: Two dozen H200 licences, some to empty offices
bodyMarkdown:
If you hold a broad index fund, Nvidia is somewhere near the top of it, and this week Washington is rewriting the rules about who is allowed to buy the company's best chips. The New York Times published an investigation on Saturday that shows why those rules are being reopened.

## What the Times found at the addresses

The U.S. Commerce Department has approved around two dozen Chinese companies to buy or manage Nvidia's H200, the company's second-strongest AI processor. The New York Times went looking for a few of them. At the listed office of New Matrix, a firm cleared this year to assemble H200s into AI servers, the Times found a small locked room with a few chairs and empty desks, and people in the building had no record of the company ever being there. Another approved firm, Maginfra, shares staff and patents with Inspur, a server maker already on the **Entity List**, the American roster of companies that U.S. firms cannot sell to without a licence. A third, Shanghai Jiatang, traces back to state-owned Datang Telecom. Commerce told the Times it reviews every application for national security risk. Nvidia said the sales support American jobs and manufacturing.

## The loophole nobody has closed

Controlling physical chips is the easy part. The harder gap is **remote access**, where a Chinese company never imports a chip at all and just rents time on one sitting in Malaysia or Ireland. Congress saw this coming. The House passed the Remote Access Security Act by 369 votes to 22 on January 12, a margin you rarely see on anything, and the bill went to the Senate Banking Committee the next day and has sat there ever since. So the executive branch is moving without it. The Information reported on Monday that the White House is weighing new controls on advanced Nvidia chips sold to China, including limits on Chinese firms reaching those chips remotely and restrictions on tooling for **lithography** machines, the equipment that prints circuit patterns onto silicon. None of it is final yet.

## What Nvidia has already written off

Nvidia reports its third quarter next Tuesday, November 17, and has guided to roughly $108 billion in revenue. The line worth reading is the one that is absent: the guidance assumes no China data centre compute revenue at all. Last quarter that same data centre business did $89 billion. So China is not what is holding this company up, and the licences at the centre of the Times story moved very few chips in practice. That gap between the political heat and the actual dollars is what I keep coming back to. CNBC reported on Sunday that Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation into Jensen Huang's relationship with a woman affiliated with Megaspeed, a cloud company and Nvidia customer accused of helping restricted Chinese firms get hold of its chips.

## The takeaway

I would watch the Senate Banking Committee more closely than the headlines. If the Remote Access Security Act finally moves, these controls get written into law and outlast whoever is in the White House, whereas rules Commerce writes on its own can be loosened as fast as they were tightened. If you own Nvidia through an index fund or a workplace pension, the thing to read next Tuesday is whether the company still assumes zero China compute revenue. A change in that single assumption, up or down, means something in Washington moved first.
